title: A Theoretically Grounded Application of Dropout in Recurrent Neural Networks
authors: Yarin Gal, Zoubin Ghahramani
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 29 (NIPS/NeurIPS 2016)
relevant_finding: Earlier work had concluded that dropout should only be used on the inputs and outputs of an RNN, because noise in the recurrent connections was thought to drown the signal. The authors derived a 'variational' dropout for LSTM and GRU networks. It samples one dropout mask per sequence and reuses it at every time step, on the inputs, the outputs and the recurrent connections. The older 'naive' approach samples a new mask at each time step and does not drop the recurrent connections. On Penn Treebank language modelling the large variational LSTM reached 73.4 test perplexity, the best single-model result at the time. That figure used MC dropout (1,000 test-time passes) and untied weights; with the standard test-time approximation it was about 75.0, against 78.4 for the earlier naive-dropout model. The best dropout rates for their method were lower than for naive dropout, even though more of the network was dropped. For the large model they were 0.3 (embeddings and recurrent connections) and 0.5 (inputs and outputs), against 0.6. For the medium model they were 0.2 and 0.35, against 0.5. On a small sentiment-analysis dataset (5,000 film reviews), the variational LSTM was the only LSTM that did not overfit. An appendix experiment found that weight decay still matters when this kind of dropout is used.
why_it_motivates: X02 sweeps the dropout rate (0, 0.1 and 0.5, against the current 0.3). This paper is the standard reference for where dropout belongs in an LSTM, and its own grid search shows the best rate depends on the model and task. In our code (ML/models/lstm.py), dropout is a separate Keras Dropout(0.3) layer after each LSTM layer. After the first layer (return_sequences=True) this draws a new mask at each time step, which is the 'naive' style, and it never touches the recurrent connections. So X02 tests only the rate of naive between-layer dropout. An optional follow-up after X02 is Keras LSTM(dropout=..., recurrent_dropout=...), which reuses one mask across time steps (the variational style). That would be a separate single change.
comparable_problem: related technique (dropout placement and rate in LSTM/GRU, tested on language modelling and sentiment classification, not EMG regression)
does_not_establish: It does not give a good dropout rate for our 1,001-parameter, 8-unit regression LSTM with 5 inputs. It does not say whether dropout helps or hurts when the target varies only about 0.4-0.8 Nm (SD), as at our plantarflexed positions. Its models were far larger (650-1,500 units per layer), used word embeddings, and did classification and language tasks. The finding that variational dropout beats naive dropout was not tested on biosignal regression.
verification_note: Independently checked. NeurIPS proceedings page confirms title, authors and NIPS 29; arXiv abstract confirms the 73.4 figure. Read the full arXiv v5 text. Sec. 1 and 5.1 describe naive vs variational masks. Footnote 3 gives the optimal rates (0.3/0.5 large and 0.2/0.35 medium, vs 0.6/0.5). Table 1 shows 73.4 is MC dropout with untied weights (75.0 tied, standard approximation). Sec. 5.2 covers the 5,000 reviews where only the variational LSTM did not overfit; Appendix B covers weight decay. Added the MC-dropout caveat and the medium-model rates. Also checked ML/models/lstm.py: Dropout(0.3) layers after LSTM(8) layers, no recurrent_dropout.

title: BiLSTM-Based Joint Torque Prediction From Mechanomyogram During Isometric Contractions: A Proof of Concept Study
authors: Jongsang Son, Fandi Shi, William Zev Rymer
venue: IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering, vol. 32, pp. 1926-1933
relevant_finding: The model predicted average isometric ankle plantarflexion torque (normalised to body mass, Nm/kg) from mechanomyogram (MMG) signals. The MMG came from a 3-axis accelerometer on the medial gastrocnemius. The networks were stacked bidirectional LSTMs, evaluated by leave-one-subject-out validation on 10 subjects, with each validation repeated 10 times. The authors crossed 4 architectures, 5 unit counts (32-512) and 4 dropout ratios (0.0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8). Dropout ratio had a significant effect on every metric (p<0.0001), but which rate was 'best' depended on the metric. Dropout 0.8 gave significantly smaller errors, but the differences were tiny (MAE 0.216 vs 0.219 Nm/kg for dropout 0.0). It also gave significantly worse regression slope and R2 (0.668 vs 0.701 for dropout 0.0). The paper is inconsistent about the dropout-0.8 slope: the text says 0.771, while Table IV says 0.701. Dropout 0.0 gave the best slope (0.857; 0.0, 0.2 and 0.5 did not differ significantly from each other) and the best R2 (0.701, significantly higher than all other rates). The interaction between unit count and dropout ratio was significant for all metrics, so the best dropout depended on network size. The final chosen model used 2 BiLSTM layers, 512 units and no dropout.
why_it_motivates: This is a close published example of a dropout sweep for LSTM torque prediction in an isometric ankle task, and it supports including 0 in X02. It also shows that heavy dropout can slightly lower average error while lowering the slope of predicted vs measured torque, so the predicted range is compressed. If that happened in our model, it could hurt the low-variance plantarflexed positions most; this is our inference, not a result of the paper. Our X02 report should therefore show per-position R2 and the predicted-vs-measured slope, not only overall MSE, because the 'best' dropout can change with the metric. The dropout-by-size interaction is a further reason not to borrow a rate tuned on large networks for our 8-unit model.
comparable_problem: comparable (isometric ankle plantarflexion torque regression with an LSTM; but the input is MMG, not surface EMG)
does_not_establish: The signals were MMG from one muscle, not 4-channel surface EMG. The model predicted one average torque per trial (many-to-one), not a continuous torque time series. Only one ankle angle was used (10 degrees plantarflexion), so the paper says nothing about the extreme plantarflexed positions. The networks were much larger (32-512 units, bidirectional, trained with Adam). Validation was across subjects, not across sessions within one subject. The error differences between dropout rates were very small, so the paper does not show that dropout meaningfully changes accuracy.
verification_note: Independently checked. Crossref and Europe PMC (PMID 38722723) confirm the metadata. Downloaded the CC-BY PDF from IEEE Xplore and read the text. I also rendered the vector tables. Table I gives the dropout ratios 0.0/0.2/0.5/0.8. Table IV gives MAE 0.219/0.222/0.221/0.216, slope 0.857/0.853/0.841/0.701 and R2 0.701/0.686/0.680/0.668. This revealed that the text gives the DR 0.8 slope as 0.771 but Table IV gives 0.701. Corrected the entry to state this and to show the error differences are tiny. Confirmed the 10x repeated LOSOCV, the MG accelerometer MMG, the single 10-degree plantarflexion angle, body-mass-normalised torque, the significant units x dropout interaction, and the final 512-unit, dropout-0.0 model. Softened 'closest' to 'close' and marked the plantarflexed-angle consequence as our inference.

title: EMG-Based Estimation of Lower Limb Joint Angles and Moments Using Long Short-Term Memory Network
authors: Minh Tat Nhat Truong, Amged Elsheikh Abdelgadir Ali, Dai Owaki, Mitsuhiro Hayashibe
venue: Sensors (MDPI), vol. 23, no. 6, article 3331
relevant_finding: The model predicted knee and ankle angles and moments (8 outputs: both sides) from 112 sEMG features (14 muscles x 8 features) in 6 healthy males. Each subject had a personalised model. It used two stacked LSTM layers of 8 hidden units each, 30% dropout, a 20-step (1 s) input window, MSE loss and batch size 8. Training used the Nadam optimiser 'with a reduced learning rate starting from 0.003 and a reduced factor of 70%' (the paper's wording; no patience is given). The authors say there is no specific rule for choosing hyperparameters and that they chose them by repeatedly adjusting and retraining. They also kept the parameter count small to avoid overfitting. Ankle moment was the hardest output: mean R2 85.44% +/- 8.14%, and only 4 of 12 ankle-moment outputs exceeded 90% R2.
why_it_motivates: Our baseline is essentially this configuration: 2 x LSTM(8), dropout 0.3, Nadam at 0.003, LR_FACTOR 0.7, batch 8 and a 20-step window (ML/models/lstm.py, ML/config.py). These values were found by trial and error for a different task. The paper reports no comparison of settings and no repeated seeds. So for our isometric, 5-input, cross-session problem they are inherited defaults, not tuned values. That is the direct reason for X02 (dropout) and X03 (learning rate). The paper's weakest output was also the ankle moment, which is consistent with ankle torque being harder to predict from EMG.
comparable_problem: comparable (sEMG to joint moment regression with a small stacked LSTM, including ankle moment)
does_not_establish: It does not show that dropout 0.3 or learning rate 0.003 is optimal, even for their own data, because no comparison is reported. Their task was dynamic (squatting, picking up an object, and sit-to-stand; the authors say walking was not covered). It used 112 EMG features and a chronological 60/20/20 split of one continuous ~5-minute recording. So it says nothing about isometric holds, low-torque plantarflexed positions, or between-session EMG changes.
verification_note: Independently checked. Read the full text via the Europe PMC full-text XML (PMC10058035; PMID 36992041); metadata matches. Confirmed the 2 x 8 units, 30% dropout, Nadam from 0.003 with a '70%' reduction factor, MSE, batch 8, 20-step window, 6 males, the trial-and-error statement, ankle-moment R2 85.44% +/- 8.14%, and 4 of 12 above 90%. Corrected an error: the earlier entry listed 'gait' among the tasks. The tasks were squat, pick-up and sit-to-stand, and the paper states walking was not covered. Reworded 'reduced by a factor of 0.7' to the paper's own phrasing. Project config (LEARNING_RATE 0.003, LR_FACTOR 0.7, BATCH_SIZE 8) checked in ML/config.py.

title: Incorporating Nesterov Momentum into Adam
authors: Timothy Dozat
venue: ICLR 2016 Workshop Track (earlier version: Stanford CS229 project report, 2015)
relevant_finding: This is the paper that introduced Nadam: Adam with its classical momentum replaced by Nesterov-style momentum. The author argues that Nesterov momentum gives a better update direction. In the CS229 version, nine optimisers were compared on three benchmarks: word2vec, an MNIST CNN, and a 2-layer, 200-cell LSTM language model. Only the learning rate differed between algorithms. Nadam beat Adam on word2vec (test loss 0.284 vs 0.325) and on the LSTM (test perplexity 105.5 vs 111.0). On the MNIST test set Adam was slightly better (0.0175 vs 0.0183). On the LSTM, plain gradient descent and classical momentum beat all adaptive methods (about 99-101 perplexity), and the author notes that tuning hyperparameters made little difference there. The author concluded that Nadam's improvement over Adam was large in most cases, but that Nadam was not always the best choice.
why_it_motivates: X03 keeps Nadam and changes only the learning rate (0.001 vs 0.003). This is the primary citation for the optimiser we use. It supports Nadam as a reasonable choice over Adam, but it does not show Nadam is the best optimiser for LSTMs, and it gives no guidance on the learning rate. That supports leaving the optimiser fixed and testing the learning rate as a single change.
comparable_problem: related technique (optimiser design; benchmarks were word embeddings, image classification and LSTM language modelling)
does_not_establish: It does not say which learning rate suits Nadam on our model, or whether 0.001 or 0.003 is better for a tiny EMG regression LSTM. The experiments were small and preliminary, single-run, with no run-to-run spread. It is a workshop paper, which had lighter review than a full conference paper.
verification_note: OpenReview (forum, PDF and API) returned a browser-challenge page, so the workshop PDF could not be opened directly. The title, author and 'Workshop track - ICLR 2016' label were confirmed from the indexed OpenReview PDF in search results. The author's GitHub README (github.com/tdozat/Optimization) asks users to cite the ICLR presentation. Read the full same-titled CS229 PDF for method and numbers: LSTM GD 100.8, Mom 99.3, NAG 99.8, Adam 111.0, Nadam 105.5; word2vec Adam 0.325, Nadam 0.284; MNIST Adam 0.0175, Nadam 0.0183. Corrected the earlier claim that Nadam's advantage was 'modest' and 'depends on the learning rate'. The author calls the gain over Adam fairly dramatic in most cases, and says tuning made little difference on the LSTM. Numbers may differ slightly in the workshop version.

title: LSTM: A Search Space Odyssey
authors: Klaus Greff, Rupesh K. Srivastava, Jan Koutnik, Bas R. Steunebrink, Juergen Schmidhuber
venue: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems, vol. 28, no. 10, pp. 2222-2232
relevant_finding: The study ran 5,400 random-search training runs: 27 searches of 200 trials, covering the standard LSTM plus 8 variants on speech (TIMIT), handwriting (IAM Online) and music (JSB Chorales) tasks. It used fANOVA to split test-performance variance across hyperparameters. The learning rate was by far the most important hyperparameter, always explaining more than two-thirds of the variance. Hidden size came second, then input noise, and momentum explained under 1%. Each dataset had a wide basin of good learning rates (up to two orders of magnitude) with little change in performance inside it. The sweet spot was at the high end of the basin, though for 2 of 3 datasets it lay outside the searched range. Interactions between hyperparameters explained 5-20% of the variance, more for TIMIT. From the small learning-rate x hidden-size interaction, the authors suggest a learning rate can be tuned on a small network and then reused on a large one. They did not test this transfer directly.
why_it_motivates: This is the main evidence that, for LSTMs, the learning rate matters more than other hyperparameters, which justifies X03 as its own experiment. It also sets expectations. 0.001 and 0.003 differ by only a factor of 3, so both may sit in the same good basin and the difference could be small. X03 therefore needs repeated seeds (see the SEEDS entries) to tell a real effect from noise. The weak interaction with hidden size also suggests a learning rate chosen in X03 is a reasonable starting point for the Tier 2 '16 units' model, though it should be rechecked there.
comparable_problem: related technique (LSTM hyperparameter importance on speech, handwriting and music sequence tasks)
does_not_establish: They trained with per-sequence SGD with Nesterov momentum, not Adam or Nadam, so the learning-rate ranges (searched from 1e-6 to 1e-2) do not transfer directly to adaptive optimisers. The tasks were classification and sequence modelling, not regression from biosignals. Their networks had 20-200 units per layer, against our 8. Dropout was not studied (they studied input noise instead).
verification_note: Independently checked. Crossref confirms vol. 28, issue 10, pp. 2222-2232, Oct 2017 and the author list. Read the arXiv full text. Sec. IV-B covers 27 searches x 200 = 5,400 runs, 9 variants, hidden size 20-200, LR 1e-6 to 1e-2 and SGD with Nesterov momentum. Sec. V-B covers: LR over two-thirds of variance, momentum under 1%, basin up to two orders of magnitude, footnote 10 (sweet spot outside range for IAM and JSB), interactions 5-20% and more important for TIMIT. The small-to-large network claim is phrased in the paper as a suggestion. Corrected '8 LSTM variants' to standard plus 8 variants, and changed 'carried over' to 'suggest', since the transfer was not directly tested.

title: Descending through a Crowded Valley - Benchmarking Deep Learning Optimizers
authors: Robin M. Schmidt, Frank Schneider, Philipp Hennig
venue: Proceedings of the 38th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2021), PMLR vol. 139, pp. 9367-9376
relevant_finding: The authors benchmarked 15 popular optimisers, including Adam and Nadam, on 8 deep-learning problems, one of them a character-level RNN. The study used 4 tuning budgets and 4 learning-rate schedules, giving 53,760 unique runs. Optimiser performance varied greatly from task to task, and no optimiser clearly won everywhere. Trying several optimisers at their default settings worked about as well as heavily tuning one. Adam, Nadam and RAdam, among others, had good default settings on several (but not all) problems, and Adam remained a strong contender. Tuning and schedules helped on average but varied widely by problem. For example, medium-budget tuning gave a median relative improvement of about 3.4% over defaults, and large-budget tuning plus a trapezoidal schedule gave about 5.2%. Tuning used a single seed, but the best setting was rerun with 10 seeds because tuning can pick 'lucky' seeds.
why_it_motivates: This recent, large benchmark supports the narrow design of X03: keep Nadam and change only the learning rate. Adaptive optimisers like Nadam often work well near their defaults, so a large gain from moving 0.003 to 0.001 should not be expected. Our setup also reduces the learning rate on plateaus (LR_FACTOR 0.7, LR_PATIENCE 10), and the paper found that schedules change outcomes in problem-specific ways. Finally, they reran the winning setting with 10 seeds, which supports running each X03 setting with several seeds before declaring a winner.
comparable_problem: related technique (optimiser and learning-rate choice across image, VAE and RNN workloads; no EMG or biomechanics)
does_not_establish: It gives no recommended learning rate for our model. Its test problems were much larger and mostly classification or generative models. The schedules tested (constant, cosine, cosine with warm restarts, trapezoidal) did not include reduce-on-plateau, which we use. It does not tell us whether the learning rate affects the low-torque plantarflexed positions differently from the strong positions.
verification_note: Independently checked. The PMLR page confirms title, authors, ICML 2021 and PMLR 139 pp. 9367-9376. Read the PMLR PDF. Confirmed: 15 optimisers, 8 problems, 4 budgets x 4 schedules, 53,760 runs; Sec. 2.3 (single tuning seed, best setting repeated with 10 seeds); Sec. 3 (Adam, Nadam, RAdam and others have well-working defaults on several but not all problems; no single best optimiser). Corrected the schedule statistic: the 5.2% median gain is for large-budget tuning plus a trapezoidal schedule vs default parameters, not for an untuned schedule alone. Medium-budget tuning without a schedule gave 3.4%.

title: Accounting for Variance in Machine Learning Benchmarks
authors: Xavier Bouthillier, Pierre Delaunay, Mirko Bronzi, Assya Trofimov, Brennan Nichyporuk, Justin Szeto, Nazanin Mohammadi Sepahvand, Edward Raff, Kanika Madan, Vikram Voleti, Samira Ebrahimi Kahou, Vincent Michalski, Tal Arbel, Chris Pal, Gael Varoquaux, Pascal Vincent
venue: Proceedings of Machine Learning and Systems 3 (MLSys 2021)
relevant_finding: The authors modelled the whole benchmarking process across 5 deep-learning case studies. Results changed noticeably with the data sample, weight initialisation, data order, dropout and hyperparameter search. Data sampling (bootstrapping the train/test split) was the largest source. Weight initialisation was generally less than half of the data-sampling variance, about the same as data order. Variance from the hyperparameter search was, on average, about as large as variance from weight initialisation. Randomising more sources of variation (not just the seed) gave a better estimate of expected performance, at 51 times less compute than the ideal estimator. Their recommendations: randomise as many sources of variation as possible; judge an improvement by the probability that A beats B in a single run rather than by the difference in means, with a suggested threshold of 0.75; and use several data splits (for example out-of-bootstrap) instead of one fixed test set.
why_it_motivates: Each X0x experiment changes one thing and compares R2 or MSE, especially at the 2 plantarflexed positions where the target varies only about 0.4-0.8 Nm (SD). There, small absolute errors cause large R2 swings, so one run per setting cannot separate a real effect from noise. This paper is the main recent reference for training each arm with several seeds and reporting the spread. It also supports paired seeds across arms and a 'probability of outperforming' style comparison. Our success criteria already do something similar: they count how many subject x position cells improved and require the gain to exceed twice the baseline's run-to-run SD.
comparable_problem: related technique (benchmarking methodology; image, NLP and medical-imaging tasks, no EMG)
does_not_establish: It does not say how many seeds our tiny LSTM needs or how big our seed-to-seed spread is; that must be measured. Their largest variance source was data sampling, but our test data is a fixed held-out session per direction (session 2 in the primary S1-to-S2 direction). Seeds alone therefore capture only part of the uncertainty they describe, and our seed spread will understate the total. The 0.75 threshold was calibrated on their 5 tasks, not on a small-subject regression study.
verification_note: Independently checked. The MLSys proceedings page confirms title, year and Proceedings of MLSys 3. The proceedings author list differs from arXiv: it gives 'Nazanin Mohammadi Sepahvand' where arXiv has 'Naz Sepah', and it omits Dmitriy Serdyuk, whom arXiv includes. The authors field now follows the proceedings page. Read the arXiv PDF. Abstract: 5 case studies, 51x cheaper. Sec. 2: initialisation generally under 50% of bootstrap variance and on par with data order; hyperparameter optimisation induces about as much variance as initialisation. Sec. 5 recommendations: randomise sources, P(A>B) with 0.75, multiple splits. Added the point that data sampling was the largest source. Corrected 'test set is session 2' to reflect both directions in EXPERIMENTS/SUCCESS_CRITERIA.md.

title: Reporting Score Distributions Makes a Difference: Performance Study of LSTM-networks for Sequence Tagging
authors: Nils Reimers, Iryna Gurevych
venue: Proceedings of the 2017 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2017), pp. 338-348
relevant_finding: The study evaluated about 50,000 LSTM networks. Changing only the random seed moved a published NER system (Lample et al.) between 89.99% and 91.00% F1 over 86 seeds, a statistically significant difference (p<1e-4). They also took 1,830 configurations and trained each twice with different seeds. The median gap was 0.17-0.72 F1 points depending on the task, and the worst case was 8.2 points (82.5% vs 74.3%). The authors recommend comparing score distributions from many runs instead of single scores. In the same study, Nadam gave the best result of six optimisers in 51.4% of 882 configurations and converged fastest (about 9 vs 42 epochs for SGD on NER). Adam, Nadam and RMSProp had about 35% lower spread than Adagrad. Variational dropout (Gal and Ghahramani) beat both naive dropout (a new mask at every time step) and no dropout in 83.5% of 479 configurations, and had the smallest spread. Applying it to both the output and recurrent connections was best in 62.6% of cases. Two stacked LSTM layers worked best (1 and 2 were on par for POS), and the number of recurrent units mattered very little.
why_it_motivates: This is the clearest LSTM-specific evidence that the seed alone can produce differences as large as a typical 'improvement'. Each X02 and X03 setting therefore needs several seeds, reported as mean +/- SD or as all individual runs. It also backs our choice of Nadam. Its 'naive dropout' (new mask every time step) matches what our Keras Dropout layer does, so it gives empirical support, beyond Gal 2016, for testing variational or recurrent dropout as a follow-up to X02.
comparable_problem: related technique (LSTM training variance and hyperparameter study on NLP sequence tagging; classification, not regression)
does_not_establish: The seed spread was measured as F1 on text-tagging tasks with much larger BiLSTM(-CRF) models (25-125 units per layer, word embeddings). So the size of the spread does not transfer to our 1,001-parameter torque regressor or to per-position R2. Their dropout rates (0.05-0.5) were tested on much larger networks. Nadam being best there does not mean it is best for EMG data.
verification_note: Independently checked. Crossref confirms EMNLP 2017, pp. 338-348 and the authors. Read the ACL Anthology PDF. Abstract: 50,000 networks. Table 1: 86 seeds, 89.99-91.00 F1, p<1e-4. Table 2: 1,830 configurations, medians 0.17-0.72%, max 8.23%, 82.5 vs 74.3. Sec. 6.2: Nadam best in 453 of 882 (51.4%), 9 vs 42 epochs, about 35% lower SD than Adagrad. Sec. 6.6: variational dropout best in 83.5% of 479, both dimensions best in 62.6%. Sec. 4.2: naive dropout defined as a new mask at every time step. Sec. 6.7: 2 stacked layers best. All stated numbers matched; no corrections needed beyond minor additions.

title: Nondeterminism and Instability in Neural Network Optimization
authors: Cecilia Summers, Michael J. Dinneen
venue: Proceedings of the 38th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2021), PMLR vol. 139, pp. 9913-9922
relevant_finding: Using 100 runs per condition, the authors varied one source of training randomness at a time: weight initialisation, data shuffling, data augmentation, GPU (cuDNN) nondeterminism, and stochastic operations such as dropout. Every source produced about the same run-to-run spread. For ResNet-14 on CIFAR-10 the test-accuracy SD was about 0.21-0.26 percentage points; for a small recurrent (QRNN) language model the perplexity SD was about 0.18-0.20. Changing a single initial weight by the smallest possible floating-point step gave about as much spread as all sources combined. The authors attribute this to training instability. Linear models did not show it (accuracy SD 0), but it appeared as soon as one hidden layer was added. Accelerated ensembling and test-time augmentation reduced the spread partly, but the authors say they are far from solving the problem.
why_it_motivates: Fixing a single seed does not remove run-to-run noise; it only hides it. Any change in X01-X06, even a different dropout rate that changes the random draws, puts the run on a different training path. A 2-layer LSTM is a non-convex network with hidden layers, so by the paper's evidence it is likely in the unstable regime. This is our inference; the paper tested CNNs and a QRNN, not LSTMs. This supports running each arm with several seeds and comparing distributions, especially for the noisy plantarflexed-position R2. Since several seeds are trained anyway, averaging their predictions (a small seed ensemble) can also be reported as a way to reduce variance at no extra training cost.
comparable_problem: related technique (training nondeterminism in image CNNs and a small recurrent language model; no EMG or regression)
does_not_establish: It does not measure the spread for our model, data or metrics, so the number of seeds we need must be estimated from our own runs. Its absolute numbers (accuracy SD, perplexity SD) cannot be converted to R2 or Nm. Our runs are single-threaded CPU TensorFlow with fixed seeds, so the cuDNN/GPU part does not apply and a given seed should be repeatable. The instability finding still means that any setting change gives a new, partly random outcome.
verification_note: Independently checked. The PMLR page confirms title, authors, ICML 2021, PMLR 139, pp. 9913-9922 (pages added). Read the PMLR PDF. Table 1 (ResNet-14/CIFAR-10, 100 runs per row): accuracy SD 0.21-0.26. Table 2 (QRNN/PTB): PPL SD 0.18-0.20, including 'stochastic operations'. Tables 3-4: random bit change 0.21 and 0.19. Sec. 4.2: linear models show SD 0; one hidden layer gives SD 0.28 (fully connected). Sec. 5: accelerated ensembling and TTA help but do not solve it. Refined the CPU note using EXPERIMENTS/reports/00_audit.md (single-thread CPU jobs, seeds 0, 1, 2). Marked the LSTM-instability point as an inference.

title: Multi-Task Learning Using Uncertainty to Weigh Losses for Scene Geometry and Semantics
authors: Alex Kendall, Yarin Gal, Roberto Cipolla
venue: IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR 2018), pp. 7482-7491
relevant_finding: Multi-task results depend strongly on how the task losses are weighted, and the best weighting depends on each task's measurement scale and noise level. The authors derive a loss that multiplies each regression task's squared error by 1/(2*sigma^2) and adds a log(sigma) penalty, with sigma (the task's noise level) learned during training. A noisier task gets a smaller weight. On a three-task benchmark (Tiny CityScapes: semantic segmentation, instance segmentation and depth), segmentation IoU was 50.1% with uniform weights, 62.8% with approximately optimal grid-searched weights and 63.4% with learned uncertainty weights. The single-task segmentation model scored 59.4%. Depth error fell from 0.640 (single task) to 0.522. A two-task comparison showed the learned weights doing slightly better than weights from a fine-grained grid search. An appendix shows the learned weights are robust to how sigma is initialised.
why_it_motivates: X04 treats each of the 8 ankle angles as a separate task. Right now the plain Nm^2 MSE is dominated by the strong angles (target std about 15 Nm, against 0.4-0.8 Nm at the plantarflexed angles). Kendall et al. are the standard reference for scaling each task's squared error by an inverse variance. They also suggest a follow-up to fixed 1/std weights: learn one log-sigma per angle.
comparable_problem: Related technique: per-task inverse-variance loss weighting in multi-task deep learning (computer vision), not EMG.
does_not_establish: Their weight is the inverse of each task's residual noise variance, not of the target's spread. Dividing our targets by each angle's std equalises scale, which is a different quantity. If the plantarflexed targets are mostly passive-torque estimation error (X01), up-weighting them will push the model to fit that noise. The paper says nothing about tiny recurrent models, about 6 subjects, or about EMG.
verification_note: Opened the arXiv abstract page and extracted the full PDF text. Confirmed equation (7), the 1/(2 sigma^2) weighting, Table 1 and the grid-search and initialisation statements. Correction: the 59.4% to 63.4% gain is against the single-task segmentation model, not against uniform weighting (50.1%) or grid-searched weights (62.8%). The benchmark is three tasks, not depth plus segmentation only. Crossref confirmed the CVPR 2018 venue and pages 7482-7491.

title: Delving into Deep Imbalanced Regression
authors: Yuzhe Yang, Kaiwen Zha, Yingcong Chen, Hao Wang, Dina Katabi
venue: Proceedings of the 38th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2021), PMLR 139:11842-11851
relevant_finding: With a continuous target, a plain loss fits the well-represented target ranges and does badly where data are sparse. On IMDB-WIKI-DIR age estimation, few-shot-region MAE was 26.33 with plain training. It fell to 22.76 with square-root inverse-frequency loss weighting (SQINV), to 22.51 with SQINV plus kernel-smoothed label density (LDS), and to 22.19 with SQINV+LDS+FDS. Many-shot MAE was essentially unchanged (7.23 plain, 7.24 SQINV, 7.20 SQINV+LDS+FDS). Full inverse-frequency weighting (INV) helped the few-shot region about as much (22.83) but hurt the many-shot region (MAE 7.64 against 7.23).
why_it_motivates: X04 assumes we can re-weight the loss to help the under-served angles without hurting the strong ones. This paper is evidence that loss reweighting can do this in deep regression. Its INV against SQINV result also matters: full inverse weighting cost accuracy in the well-served region, while the square-root version did not. That argues for testing 1/sqrt(std) alongside full 1/std per-angle weights.
comparable_problem: Related technique: reweighting by target density in deep imbalanced regression (images, text, health data), not EMG.
does_not_establish: Their imbalance is rare target values. Ours is a group (angle) whose targets have a tiny spread. Small torques are actually common at every angle, so their density-based weights would not single out the plantarflexed angles. Results come from large datasets and big CNNs (ResNet-50 for IMDB-WIKI-DIR), not a ~1,000-parameter LSTM trained on 6 subjects.
verification_note: Opened the PMLR proceedings page (title, authors, volume and pages confirmed) and extracted the arXiv PDF text. Read Table 1 and the full appendix IMDB-WIKI-DIR table directly. Correction: the original said the gain came 'especially after LDS'. In fact LDS added only a small further gain (22.76 to 22.51). Added the INV many-shot cost (7.64 against 7.23) from the appendix table.

title: Density-based weighting for imbalanced regression
authors: Michael Steininger, Konstantin Kobs, Padraig Davidson, Anna Krause, Andreas Hotho
venue: Machine Learning, 110(8), 2187-2211
relevant_finding: DenseLoss weights each training sample by how rare its target value is, using kernel density estimation. A single hyperparameter, alpha, sets how strong the weighting is: alpha = 0 gives uniform weights, i.e. ordinary MSE. The weights are rescaled to a mean of 1 so the learning rate does not need retuning. On synthetic data, alpha = 1 cut RMSE in the rarest bin by 1.21-7.02, but raised it in the most common bin by 1.12-1.68. Alpha above 1 hurt common bins badly, and sometimes the rarest bin too. Across 20 benchmark datasets, normalised MAE fell by roughly 10% for rare points while error rose for common points. DenseLoss mostly beat the SMOGN resampling method. As future work, the authors propose ensembles of models trained with different alpha values, each an expert for part of the target range.
why_it_motivates: X04 should be run as a dial, not an on/off switch. For example, weight each angle by std^(-alpha) with alpha in {0, 0.5, 1}, rescale the weights to a mean of 1, and report per-angle R2 for each setting so the trade-off between strong and weak angles is visible. Their 'expert per target range' idea also ties X04 to the Tier 2 per-angle-experts plan.
comparable_problem: Related technique: cost-sensitive (weighted) loss for imbalanced regression with neural networks. Applications include precipitation downscaling, not EMG.
does_not_establish: It weights by how rare each target value is, not by angle group or target scale. It gives no evidence that weighting helps when the under-served group's targets are partly measurement noise, which the passive-torque errors may make ours. It shows the opposite of a free lunch: with alpha = 1, accuracy on the common cases got measurably worse, so X04 may cost accuracy at the strong angles.
verification_note: Crossref confirmed the metadata (Machine Learning 110(8):2187-2211, 2021). Extracted and read the full open-access PDF from the Wuerzburg repository: abstract, weighting function, Section 4.1.3 results, the 20-dataset SMOGN comparison and the conclusion. Correction: the original said the paper 'does not show the trade-off costs nothing'. The paper actually reports an explicit cost on common bins (+1.12 to +1.68 RMSE at alpha = 1). Numbers added.

title: Do Current Multi-Task Optimization Methods in Deep Learning Even Help?
authors: Derrick Xin, Behrooz Ghorbani, Justin Gilmer, Ankush Garg, Orhan Firat
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (NeurIPS 2022), Main Conference Track, pp. 13597-13609
relevant_finding: The authors compared specialised multi-task loss-balancing optimisers (MGDA, GradNorm, PCGrad, IMTL, random loss weighting) with a fixed weighted sum of task losses, on translation, CityScapes and CelebA. None of the specialised methods beat a tuned fixed weighting. On translation they only landed on other points of the fixed-weight trade-off curve, and their learned task weights barely moved during training. For generalisation, some fixed weightings beat all the specialised methods. On CityScapes the segmentation loss was about 10 times larger than the depth loss, and most of the best-generalising models gave segmentation a weight below 0.2. On CelebA, tuning learning rate and weight decay mattered more than which balancing method was used. Under-tuned baselines can create false gains.
why_it_motivates: Supports keeping X04 simple: fixed per-angle weights set from the training data (inverse std, or a small sweep of the exponent). A learned or adaptive weighting scheme is not needed. The CityScapes result directly supports down-weighting the task whose loss dominates. The paper also warns that the unweighted baseline must get the same tuning effort (X02/X03 settings), or any X04 gain could just be under-tuning.
comparable_problem: Related technique: how to weight several losses in multi-task deep learning (language and vision), not EMG.
does_not_establish: It does not say which fixed weights are right for our angles, or whether weighting helps at all with 6 subjects and a tiny LSTM. Its experiments use large models and datasets. The main translation study did not include Kendall-style uncertainty weighting among the methods compared.
verification_note: Opened the NeurIPS 2022 proceedings page (the original '-Abstract.html' link also loads) and the arXiv page, and extracted the full PDF text. Confirmed the methods compared, the translation results, the CityScapes loss-imbalance finding and the CelebA tuning finding. Crossref confirmed DOI 10.52202/068431-0988 and pages 13597-13609. The author order follows the proceedings; arXiv lists Gilmer last. The original 'hyperparameter-grid choices mattered more' claim holds for CelebA specifically.

title: Consensus for experimental design in electromyography (CEDE) project: Amplitude normalization matrix
authors: Manuela Besomi, Paul W. Hodges, Edward A. Clancy, Jaap Van Dieen, Francois Hug, Madeleine Lowery, Roberto Merletti, Karen Sogaard, Tim Wrigley, Thor Besier, Richard G. Carson, Catherine Disselhorst-Klug, Roger M. Enoka, Deborah Falla, Dario Farina, Simon Gandevia, Ales Holobar, Matthew C. Kiernan, Kevin McGill, Eric Perreault, John C. Rothwell, Kylie Tucker
venue: Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology, 53, 102438
relevant_finding: This international expert consensus says amplitude normalisation is what makes comparisons across participants, muscles, sessions and electrode positions meaningful, because raw amplitude depends on muscle and tissue properties. It reviews six reference options with pros and cons: task-specific MVC, standardised isometric MVC, standardised submaximal task, peak or mean EMG during the task, no normalisation, and maximal M-wave. It advises choosing the reference to match how the EMG will be interpreted, and checking how normalised values may change under particular conditions. For peak/mean-in-task normalisation it lists a key drawback: every signal is set relative to its own peak or mean, so it reduces variation between sessions, but a muscle working at 5% of maximum cannot be told apart from one working at 100%, and real changes in the peak are hidden.
why_it_motivates: X05 replaces the fixed session-1 scaling with a reference recomputed from each session's own EMG (per-muscle running percentiles). That is a data-driven form of the 'peak/mean EMG during the task' reference described in the matrix. The paper is the current standard citation for why raw amplitude should not be carried from one session to the next. It also names the main risk of X05.
comparable_problem: Related technique: EMG amplitude-normalisation methodology (a consensus paper, no prediction model).
does_not_establish: It reports no data on how normalisation affects an ML torque model's accuracy between sessions. Its own list of cons warns that peak/mean-in-task normalisation removes absolute activation level. So if session 2 genuinely contains stronger or weaker contractions, a running-percentile reference will partly erase the torque information X05 needs to keep. It does not say how long a normalisation window should be for ML inputs.
verification_note: Europe PMC confirmed the title, all 22 authors, journal, volume 53, article 102438 and PMID 32569878. This time I also extracted and read the publisher's PDF from the VU Amsterdam repository (research.vu.nl), including the abstract and the peak/mean pros-and-cons table. Corrections: removed the claim that electrode re-positioning is the paper's 'main concern'. Replaced the claim that the consensus 'does not address' shifting references: it explicitly lists that drawback for peak/mean normalisation.

title: Sliding-Window Normalization to Improve the Performance of Machine-Learning Models for Real-Time Motion Prediction Using Electromyography
authors: Taichi Tanaka, Isao Nambu, Yoshiko Maruyama, Yasuhiro Wada
relevant_finding: Each EMG sample is z-scored using the mean and std of the most recent window (100-500 ms tested; 200-500 ms recommended), so it runs causally with no calibration step. Ten subjects did 12 elbow-movement conditions, and a logistic regression classified rest/flexion/extension. For the subject's own model, accuracy was 77.7% with sliding-window normalisation, 56.2% with none and 77.2% with a fixed z-score from training data (sliding vs fixed not significantly different). For models trained on 9 other subjects, it gave 63.1%, against 41.4% with none and 54.4% with fixed z-score (significant). The authors expect normalisation to be affected when EMG changes across days, with sensor placement or with fatigue, but did not test this.
why_it_motivates: This is the closest published version of X05's idea: normalise each channel with running statistics instead of statistics frozen from the training data. Fixed normalisation fell behind only when the data distribution changed (other subjects), the same kind of shift as our session-to-session amplitude change. With no shift it gave no gain.
comparable_problem: Related technique: running/sliding-window EMG normalisation, used for classifying movements, not regressing torque.
does_not_establish: It is classification, where relative patterns are enough. In torque regression the absolute envelope level carries the torque information. A short window (hundreds of ms, near the contraction length) would normalise away the contraction level itself, so X05's window has to be much longer than one contraction. Own-subject train and test trials were assigned at random in blocks of 10 trials from the same recordings, with no across-day test, so the cross-session benefit is untested. Regression is listed only as future work.
verification_note: Read the full text via Europe PMC (PMC9269700). Checked the method (causal trailing window, fixed z-score from training data), subjects, accuracy numbers and the limitation statement. Correction: the split was random blocks of 10 consecutive trials across 10 recording sessions, not a random split 'within one recording'. Added that the own-subject gain over fixed z-score was not significant. Note: the paper itself has small internal inconsistencies (77.7 +/- 2.2 vs +/- 2.9). Crossref metadata matched.

title: Multi-Day EMG-Based Knee Joint Torque Estimation Using Hybrid Neuromusculoskeletal Modelling and Convolutional Neural Networks
authors: Robert V. Schulte, Marijke Zondag, Jaap H. Buurke, Erik C. Prinsen
venue: Frontiers in Robotics and AI, 9, 869476
relevant_finding: Ten able-bodied participants did seated, non-weight-bearing knee and ankle movements on days 1, 2, 3 and 7. EMG was MVC-normalised, with MVC re-measured before each session. Models were trained on day 1 only and tested on a held-out 20% of day-1 data and on all later-day data. The CNN (convolution plus LSTM) knee-torque NRMSE rose from 5.8% on day 1 to 10.0-11.0% on days 2-7. The hybrid CNN-musculoskeletal model rose from 10.0% to 12.6-14.1%. Both differed significantly between day 1 and the later days, but days 2, 3 and 7 did not differ from each other. Only the musculoskeletal model (13.4-15.2% on all days) showed no significant between-day change. The CNN still had the lowest error on every day. The authors suggest electrode placement and day-to-day MVC differences as possible causes but did not test them.
why_it_motivates: This is the closest comparable result: an EMG-to-torque deep model trained on one session loses accuracy on a later session, even with per-session MVC normalisation. It motivates X05 (making the input scaling adapt to each session) and supports reporting session-2 results separately rather than pooling.
comparable_problem: Comparable: EMG-envelope-to-joint-torque regression with a deep model, trained on one session and tested on others.
does_not_establish: Sessions were on different days, probably with electrodes re-applied (the paper does not say), and the task involved dynamic knee movement. Our two sessions are on the same visit with electrodes left on, so our shift should be smaller. Part of the day-1 advantage may come from testing on held-out data from the training session itself, not only from amplitude drift. The study does not isolate amplitude change as the cause, and it does not test running or adaptive normalisation.
verification_note: Opened the full article on frontiersin.org and confirmed the title, authors, volume, article number, DOI, design (days 1/2/3/7, trained on day 1 with an 80/20 split), the per-day NRMSE table, the statistics and the discussion. Added that the CNN still outperformed the other models on later days, that days 2-7 did not differ from each other, and the within-session test-set caveat.

title: Surface EMG-Based Inter-Session Gesture Recognition Enhanced by Deep Domain Adaptation
authors: Yu Du, Wenguang Jin, Wentao Wei, Yu Hu, Weidong Geng
venue: Sensors, 17(3), 458
relevant_finding: Their fix for session-to-session shift is adaptive batch normalisation (AdaBN): keep every trained weight fixed and only re-estimate the normalisation statistics on unlabeled data from the new session. Inter-session accuracy (majority-voted) rose from 62.7% to 82.3% on CSL-HDEMG and from 47.9% to 63.3% on CapgMyo DB-b. Per-frame accuracy rose from 29.3% to 35.4% and from 35.0% to 41.2%. On CSL-HDEMG the gain peaked using only about 5% (roughly 10 s) of the new session's unlabeled data.
why_it_motivates: This is the main deep-learning evidence that much of the inter-session drop sits in the input statistics and can be fixed just by re-normalising with the new session's own unlabeled EMG. That is what X05 does with per-muscle running percentiles. It also suggests a simple X05 variant: recompute per-muscle scaling from the first ~10 s of session 2 and keep the model fixed.
comparable_problem: Related technique: unsupervised inter-session domain adaptation for EMG (gesture classification, high-density EMG).
does_not_establish: It covers classification with high-density arrays. CapgMyo DB-b's electrodes were re-applied at slightly different positions more than a week apart, a much larger shift than ours. The main results re-estimated statistics on the whole test session, which is not causal. Our LSTM has no batch-norm layers, so the analogy is to input scaling. It is older than 5 years, but it is the standard reference for this idea in EMG.
verification_note: Read the full text via Europe PMC (PMC5375744). Confirmed the metadata, the AdaBN method, that the main results used the entire unlabeled test session, the ~5% (~10 s) calibration result (run on CSL-HDEMG, Figure 7), and the Table 4 numbers (62.7/82.3 and 47.9/63.3 majority-voted; 29.3/35.4 and 35.0/41.2 per frame).

title: Improved Surface Electromyogram-Based Hand-Wrist Force Estimation Using Deep Neural Networks and Cross-Joint Transfer Learning
authors: Wang H, Wang H, Dai C, Huang X, Clancy EA
relevant_finding: Nine subjects tracked a random force target at a fixed hand-wrist posture. The authors tried eight input window lengths (98, 195, 293, 391, 488, 586, 684 and 781 ms) with linear regression, an MLP, an LSTM, a CNN and a CNN-LSTM. This window comparison was done without transfer learning, using two-fold cross-validation on the hand-wrist trials. Error fell as the window grew from 98 ms and levelled off after about 293-391 ms. Windows longer than 391 ms gave no significant further improvement (p > 0.061). The best windows were 586 ms for the CNN (5.24 %MVT), 488 ms for the LSTM (6.10 %MVT) and 684 ms for the MLP (6.44 %MVT), but none of these was significantly better than 391 ms. The deep models needed shorter windows than linear regression: the CNN at 98 ms (7.02 %MVT) matched linear regression at 391 ms (7.19 %MVT). The authors conclude that the dependencies between sEMG and force are short-term (under 400 ms).
why_it_motivates: This is the most direct support for X06 (0.2 s vs 0.4 s). In a similar EMG-to-force regression, error was still falling around 0.2 s and levelled off by about 0.3-0.4 s. So 0.4 s is a sensible upper test value, and going much longer is unlikely to help. One caveat: the paper describes the trend (improvement up to 293-391 ms, then a plateau) but does not report a direct test of 195 ms against 391 ms.
comparable_problem: Comparable: sEMG to force/torque regression with neural networks, including an LSTM, at a fixed posture.
does_not_establish: This is an upper-limb task (hand-wrist, with elbow data used only as the transfer-learning source). Subjects tracked a random force target, the evaluation was within a session, and error was reported in %MVT. It says nothing about whether a longer window helps at weak, plantarflexed ankle angles where torque varies by less than 1 Nm. It also does not show whether a longer window fixes problems caused by passive-torque errors or by EMG amplitude drift between sessions.
verification_note: I re-checked metadata and the abstract against the Europe PMC record. In the Europe PMC full-text XML (PMC11598622) I confirmed the window lengths, the per-model minima, the p > 0.061 plateau, the 9 subjects, the 98-ms CNN vs 391-ms linear regression comparison and the 'stabilized after 293-391 ms' wording. I softened the claim that 0.2 to 0.3-0.4 s 'still reduced error', because the paper gives no pairwise test for that step.

title: Multimodal Estimation of Endpoint Force During Quasi-Dynamic and Dynamic Muscle Contractions Using Deep Learning
authors: Hajian G, Morin E, Etemad A
venue: IEEE Transactions on Instrumentation and Measurement 71:1-11
relevant_finding: In 16 healthy subjects, a multimodal CNN used high-density EMG and IMU data to estimate force during elbow flexion and extension. Three segment lengths were compared (50, 100 and 150 ms, with 50% overlap; intra-subject validation R²). The shortest segment was best in every condition. Isotonic R² was 0.98, 0.97 and 0.92; isokinetic R² was 0.96, 0.90 and 0.83; dynamic R² was 0.96, 0.92 and 0.82. 50 ms was significantly better than 150 ms in every condition. For isotonic contractions only, 50 ms and 100 ms did not differ significantly. The authors also cite earlier isometric work (Nielsen et al.) that found no significant difference for windows of 100 ms or longer.
why_it_motivates: This is the counter-evidence for X06: a longer window is not automatically better. When force changes quickly, shorter segments tracked it better. Even in the steadier isotonic condition, 150 ms was worse than 50 ms. The 'little difference above about 100 ms in isometric contractions' point comes from the Nielsen study they cite, not from their own data. Together this makes 0.4 s vs 0.2 s a genuinely uncertain single change, and per-angle results should be checked, not just the average.
comparable_problem: Comparable: EMG (plus IMU) to force regression with deep learning. However, the contractions were isotonic, isokinetic and dynamic, not isometric.
does_not_establish: The windows tested were only 50-150 ms, so the paper does not test 0.2 s vs 0.4 s at all. Their 'segment' is a raw-signal input window for a CNN that makes one prediction per segment, not the look-back length of an LSTM over smoothed envelopes. With 50% overlap, longer segments also give fewer training samples; this is my inference, not something the authors tested. The results are for the elbow and for moving contractions, so they do not carry over directly to our slow isometric ankle trials or to the low-torque plantarflexed angles.
verification_note: I confirmed journal, volume, pages and DOI through Crossref. From the arXiv HTML full text I confirmed the 16 participants, the Table VI R² values for all three conditions, the significance statements and the Nielsen citation. I added the isotonic numbers and the fact that the windows were only 50-150 ms. I also made clear that the isometric 'no difference above 100 ms' result is a cited prior study, not this paper's own finding.

title: Determining the optimal window length for pattern recognition-based myoelectric control: balancing the competing effects of classification error and controller delay
authors: Smith LH, Hargrove LJ, Lock BA, Kuiken TA
venue: IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering 19(2):186-192
relevant_finding: Thirteen able-bodied subjects controlled a virtual upper-limb prosthesis using EMG pattern recognition. The classifiers used analysis windows from 50 to 550 ms, with 2 or 4 channels. Offline, classification error fell as the window got longer (p < 0.01). In real-time use, user performance improved with lower classification error but got worse with longer controller delay (both p < 0.01). For their system the best window was 150-250 ms. This is a widely cited reference for the trade-off between accuracy and delay when choosing an EMG window length.
why_it_motivates: This is the foundational framing for X06. A longer window usually lowers offline error but adds lag if the model is ever used in real time. It also supports 0.2 s as a conventional baseline, since 0.2 s falls inside their best range. If 0.4 s only helps offline, the report should mention the lag cost.
comparable_problem: Related technique: choosing the window length for EMG decoding. The problem is different: classifying movements for prosthesis control rather than regressing torque.
does_not_establish: This is a classification study, not continuous torque regression, and it used upper-limb control of a virtual prosthesis. The best window depends on the controller and the task. It does not tell us the best LSTM look-back for isometric ankle torque, or whether a causal LSTM predicting at the last sample would suffer the same delay.
verification_note: I re-confirmed title, authors, volume, issue, pages, DOI and all the abstract statements (50-550 ms, 13 subjects, p-values, 150-250 ms optimum) against the Europe PMC record. No changes were needed beyond small wording edits.

title: Influence of Joint Angle on EMG-Torque Model During Constant-Posture, Torque-Varying Contractions
authors: Liu P, Liu L, Clancy EA
venue: IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering 23(6):1039-1046
relevant_finding: In 22 subjects, biceps and triceps sEMG were related to elbow torque at six fixed elbow angles (60-135 degrees). Posture was held constant while torque varied. The authors compared three nonlinear EMG-torque models. Separate per-angle models gave the lowest error: 4.01 ± 1.2%, expressed as a percentage of the MVC measured at 90 degrees of flexion. Those per-angle models could not interpolate between angles. The best model that could interpolate across angles was statistically equivalent, at 4.06 ± 1.2%. Better EMG amplitude processing (whitened, multi-channel) and longer training data both improved accuracy.
why_it_motivates: This is the key reference for Tier 2. The EMG-torque relationship changes with joint angle. Per-angle models (experts) and one model that takes angle into account and can interpolate gave equally good results. That supports trying an explicitly angle-conditioned model (for example, an angle-dependent gain) as a cheaper alternative to a full set of experts. The finding that longer training data helps is also a warning: splitting six subjects' data into per-angle experts may leave each expert with too little data.
comparable_problem: Comparable: sEMG to joint torque regression at several fixed joint angles, with torque varying at each posture.
does_not_establish: This study is on the elbow, not the ankle, and used classical nonlinear EMG-torque models rather than an LSTM. All errors are scaled to a single MVC (at 90 degrees). That means a pooled score can hide poor relative accuracy at weak angles, which is exactly our failure mode. It does not show what happens at angles where torque varies by less than 1 Nm.
verification_note: I re-confirmed metadata and the abstract numbers (22 subjects, six angles, 4.01 vs 4.06% MVC(F90), statistically equivalent) in the Europe PMC record. The full text is not in PMC and was not opened, so the exact form of the model that interpolates across angles is not confirmed. I clarified that the error is relative to the MVC at 90 degrees of flexion.

title: Effects of Changes in Ankle Joint Angle on the Relation Between Plantarflexion Torque and EMG Magnitude in Major Plantar Flexors of Male Chronic Stroke Survivors
authors: Son J, Rymer WZ
venue: Frontiers in Neurology 11:224
relevant_finding: Nine male chronic stroke survivors held isometric plantarflexion at 0, 20, 40 and 60% MVIC (5-s holds; the target was set from MG EMG feedback). They did this at five ankle angles, from maximum plantarflexion to maximum dorsiflexion, on both legs. For each muscle (MG, LG, SOL), the slope of EMG against torque was fitted at each angle. EMG was the RMS over a steady 1-s segment. The slope increased as the ankle became more plantarflexed, on both the paretic and the non-paretic side. The authors fitted this as S = aA² + b, with A measured from maximum dorsiflexion. On the non-paretic side the median reported a was 0.655 for MG, 0.740 for LG and 0.258 for SOL (true values are 1000 times smaller; n = 8 for SOL). Maximum torque was larger at dorsiflexed angles than at plantarflexed angles (p = 0.029). The authors explain that at shorter muscle lengths the torque produced for a given EMG is smaller. They interpret the steeper slope as lower contraction efficiency.
why_it_motivates: This gives a physiological reason for Tier 2. At plantarflexed ankle angles the triceps surae produce less torque for the same EMG, even on the non-paretic side. So the EMG-to-torque gain depends on angle and is lowest at the angles where our model fails. Our hypothesis, not tested by the paper, is that an unconditioned or weakly conditioned 8-unit LSTM may average this gain across angles and over-predict at plantarflexed angles. That argues for an angle-conditioned gain or per-angle experts.
comparable_problem: Comparable (physiology): the EMG-torque relationship of the ankle plantarflexors across fixed ankle angles in isometric contractions. No ML model is involved.
does_not_establish: The subjects were male stroke survivors. The non-paretic leg is the closest to healthy but is not a healthy control. Slopes came from a linear fit to a few discrete steady holds (RMS EMG, 500-ms window), not from continuously tracked envelopes. The paper does not describe subtracting passive torque. (A constant passive offset at each angle would not change a fitted slope anyway, but this is my reasoning, not the paper's.) It tests no estimator, so it cannot show that angle conditioning will fix our R² drop.
verification_note: I re-read the Europe PMC full-text XML (PMC7155781) and confirmed the five angles, the 0/20/40/60% MVIC levels, S = aA² + b with A shifted from maximum dorsiflexion, the Table 1 medians and the x1000 footnote, and p = 0.029. The axis direction (higher slope means more EMG per unit torque) is now confirmed by the authors' own sentence that torque at shorter lengths is smaller at a given EMG. Note that the paper's angle sign convention is internally inconsistent: Methods says positive = dorsiflexion, while the Figure 4 caption says negative = dorsiflexion. The direction of the main finding is clear from the abstract. I softened 'depends strongly' and marked the over-prediction idea as our hypothesis.

experiment: Tier 2 (angle-conditioned model); also relevant to X05
title: Influence of Input Features and EMG Type on Ankle Joint Torque Prediction With Support Vector Regression
authors: Kizyte A, Lei Y, Wang R
venue: IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering 31:4286-4294
relevant_finding: HD-EMG from five lower-leg muscles (TA, soleus, MG, LG and peroneus longus), plus a bipolar signal made from two central electrodes of each grid, was used to predict ankle torque 100 ms ahead with SVR. Five subjects did isometric dorsi- and plantarflexion following slow trapezoid torque targets at 30, 50 and 70% MVC. This was repeated at four ankle angles: 15 and 7.5 degrees plantarflexion, 0 degrees, and 10 degrees dorsiflexion. Seven other subjects did dynamic tasks. All HD-EMG inputs gave significantly more accurate isometric torque than bipolar EMG (p ≤ 0.01). According to the first author's thesis summary (Table 4.1), isometric NRMSE was 0.04 (HD-EMG) and 0.06 (bipolar) in the 'intra-session' case. That case trained and tested with 5-fold cross-validation on repetitions within one trial, meaning one angle, one level and one direction. NRMSE was 0.06 and 0.10 in the 'inter-session' case, which trained on all other trials of the subject and tested on one held-out trial. For dynamic tasks, good prediction needed added ankle angle and angular velocity. Kinematic inputs were used only in the dynamic protocol.
why_it_motivates: This is the closest ankle-specific comparison for Tier 2. Predicting a whole held-out angle-level trial from the other trials was clearly harder than predicting new repetitions within the same trial, and the drop was larger for bipolar EMG, which is what we use (0.06 to 0.10). That fits the idea that the EMG-torque mapping shifts across angle and level, so pooled models do not transfer perfectly. Per-angle experts or stronger angle conditioning are therefore worth testing. It is not, however, a clean head-to-head test of per-angle models against a pooled model.
comparable_problem: Comparable: EMG to ankle torque regression in isometric contractions at several fixed ankle angles, with the triceps surae and TA.
does_not_establish: The model is SVR, not an LSTM, and only five isometric subjects were tested. Their 'inter-session' case was leave-one-trial-out within one session, not a second recording session, so it says nothing about EMG amplitude drift between days (X05). Their 'intra-session' case tested on the same trial it was trained on, so the gap mixes 'unseen condition' with 'unseen trial'. Plantarflexion went only to 15 degrees. Torque was normalised to MVC with no stated passive correction. NRMSE was divided by the range of the measured torque. It does not report accuracy for each angle, so we cannot tell how it behaved at the weakest angles. It also did not test adding ankle angle as an input for isometric prediction.
verification_note: I confirmed metadata and abstract through Europe PMC and Semantic Scholar (gold open access, CC BY). The IEEE full text was blocked (HTTP 418). I re-read the first author's KTH licentiate thesis (DiVA diva2:1735749), which summarises this paper as Paper I. From it I confirmed the 5 isometric subjects, the angles and MVC levels, the bipolar derivation from the grid, the 100-ms-ahead SVR, the definitions of each evaluation case, the NRMSE formula and the Table 4.1 values. I corrected an overstatement: intra-session vs inter-session is not a per-angle-vs-pooled comparison. I also removed the claim that the HD-EMG/bipolar gap points to cross-session amplitude variability. The published article's own tables were not checked directly.

title: Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts
authors: Jacobs RA, Jordan MI, Nowlan SJ, Hinton GE
venue: Neural Computation 3(1):79-87
relevant_finding: This paper introduced a training method for systems built from several separate 'expert' networks, each learning to handle a subset of the training cases. A gating network decides, for each input, which expert to use, and the gate and experts are trained together. The error function makes the experts compete rather than cooperate, so each expert specialises in a local region of the input space. On a vowel discrimination task the system split the problem into subtasks that each very simple expert could solve. The authors contrast this with earlier work in which each expert was trained separately on a subtask assigned in advance.
why_it_motivates: This is the original reference for the Tier 2 'per-angle experts' idea. Because our condition (ankle angle) is known, the gate can either be fixed by angle (hard per-angle experts, which is closer to the pre-assigned subtasks the paper contrasts with) or learned (a soft mixture, as in this paper). Either way, the weak plantarflexed angles could get their own mapping instead of sharing one dominated by the strong angles.
comparable_problem: Related technique: the same method (modular experts with gating), applied to a different problem (vowel classification).
does_not_establish: It gives no evidence about EMG or torque regression, about small datasets (6 subjects, a model of about 1,000 parameters) or about within-subject cross-session tests. Splitting data across experts reduces the data each expert sees, and the paper does not show whether that trade-off pays off at angles where torque varies very little.
verification_note: I confirmed title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and abstract through Crossref. I also viewed page 80 of the scanned PDF (Hinton's site), which confirms the gating network, the competitive error function and the contrast with experts trained separately on pre-assigned subtasks.

title: Estimation of Joint Torque by EMG-Driven Neuromusculoskeletal Models and LSTM Networks
authors: Zhang L, Soselia D, Wang R, Gutierrez-Farewik EM
venue: IEEE Transactions on Neural Systems and Rehabilitation Engineering 31:3722-3731
relevant_finding: The authors estimated ankle dorsi/plantarflexion, knee flexion/extension, hip flexion/extension and hip abduction/adduction torques from EMG plus kinematics during 10 daily movements. They used EMG-driven neuromusculoskeletal (NMS) models and LSTM networks, with inverse-dynamics torque as ground truth. Three setups were compared: Pooled (one model for all movements), Individual (one model per movement) and Clustered (one model per group of similar movements). The abstract says the Pooled, Individual and Clustered LSTMs all had relatively high accuracy. For NMS models, the Individual and Clustered versions did similarly well, while the Pooled NMS model 'may be too generic'. Clustering improved NMS accuracy in some movements but made relatively little difference for the LSTMs, which were already accurate.
why_it_motivates: This establishes LSTMs as a standard, competitive tool for estimating joint torque from EMG, including at the ankle. It also gives a direct comparison for Tier 2: for LSTMs, splitting by condition (per-movement or per-cluster models) made little difference compared with one pooled model. So per-angle experts are not guaranteed to help, and the result should be compared against a pooled, angle-conditioned LSTM.
comparable_problem: Comparable: EMG (plus kinematics) to lower-limb joint torque with LSTM networks, including ankle plantar/dorsiflexion torque.
does_not_establish: The task was dynamic daily movements with inverse-dynamics torque, not isometric voluntary torque with passive torque removed. The LSTMs also received kinematics, which gives them condition information our model may lack. The abstract gives no numbers and no results for low-variance conditions. The pooled-vs-individual comparison was across movements, not ankle angles. Network size was not checked, so the result should not be assumed to hold for an 8-unit LSTM.
verification_note: I re-confirmed metadata and the full abstract text in Europe PMC (the abstract sentences match). The article is gold open access (CC BY) according to Crossref and Semantic Scholar, but IEEE Xplore returned HTTP 418, so the full text was not read and no numbers are reported. I changed 'was too generic' to the abstract's 'may be too generic' and replaced the guess that the networks were 'likely far larger' with an explicit note that size was not checked.

experiment: Context (deep learning for EMG-based torque/force estimation)
title: Deep Learning for EMG-based Human-Machine Interaction: A Review
authors: Xiong D, Zhang D, Zhao X, Zhao Y
venue: IEEE/CAA Journal of Automatica Sinica 8(3):512-533

does_not_establish: As a broad review it gives no evidence for any specific fix we plan (window length, per-angle weighting, angle conditioning). It does not address passive-torque subtraction or low-variance targets at weak angles.
