title: Time course of stress relaxation and recovery in human ankles
authors: Duong B, Low M, Moseley AM, Lee RYW, Herbert RD
venue: Clinical Biomechanics 16(7):601-607
relevant_finding: In experiment 1 (n=8), relaxed ankles were held at a fixed dorsiflexion angle for 20 min, released for 2 min, then stretched again. In experiment 2 (n=24), a 20-min stretch was followed by a release of 0 to 20 min and a second stretch. Torque was recorded continuously. During a constant-angle stretch, passive torque fell bi-exponentially towards a fitted asymptote of 58% of its starting value, so the largest possible drop was about 42%. Getting half of that drop took nearly 5 min. Within 2 min of release, torque had recovered by 43% (the abstract's figure). Recovery did not appear to differ between subjects who stayed relaxed during the release and those who did isometric contractions. Recovery followed a time course similar to the relaxation.
why_it_motivates: X01: Passive torque at a fixed angle is not one fixed number. It depends on how long the joint has been held at that angle and on what happened in the previous few minutes. A passive value from a separate passive trial recorded earlier may therefore differ from the passive torque actually present during the active trial (our inference). This supports building the cleaned passive table from a consistent time window, such as the same point in every hold or the rest period just before each contraction.
comparable_problem: Related technique: measuring passive ankle torque on a dynamometer. It is not an EMG-to-torque regression study.
does_not_establish: It does not give the size of stress relaxation at strongly plantarflexed angles. There the passive torque is small and comes mainly from different structures, the stretched dorsiflexors and front-of-ankle tissues rather than the calf (general knowledge, not from this paper). The 58% asymptote comes from a 20-min hold in the dorsiflexed range, so it does not tell us how big the drop is in the short holds used for a passive table. It does not show how much error this causes in our voluntary-torque targets or in the LSTM's R2.
verification_note: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages and DOI confirmed from the PubMed record (PMID 11470302). All numbers (n=8 and n=24, bi-exponential decline to a 58% asymptote, nearly 5 min to half of maximal relaxation, 43% recovery within 2 min, no apparent difference between relaxed and contracting subjects during release) checked against the full PubMed abstract. Full text not opened because it is paywalled and the Brighton repository link returned a web page, not the PDF. Correction: the original said torque 'dropped by about 42% overall'. The 42% is the fitted maximum possible drop, not the measured drop. Related paper found while checking: McNair PJ, Dombroski EW, Hewson DJ, Stanley SN (2001) Med Sci Sports Exerc 33(3):354-358, PMID 11252058. With the ankle at 80% of maximal dorsiflexion range, force fell 21.5%, 21.7% and 19% across the 4x15-s, 2x30-s and 1x60-s hold conditions, with most of the drop in the first 20 s of a hold. It is the better reference for short holds if the orchestrator wants to swap one in.

title: Isometric contractions reduce plantar flexor moment, Achilles tendon stiffness, and neuromuscular activity but remove the subsequent effects of stretch
authors: Kay AD, Blazevich AJ
venue: Journal of Applied Physiology 107(4):1181-1189
relevant_finding: 16 healthy adults were tested on an isokinetic dynamometer before and after six 8-s maximal isometric plantar flexor contractions. After the contractions, passive ankle joint moment was 4.9% lower and Achilles tendon stiffness 10.9% lower (both P<0.01). Isometric maximal moment did not fall. Peak concentric moment fell 11.5%, and peak triceps surae EMG amplitude fell 21.0%, the two drops being correlated (r=0.90). Three 60-s static stretches done next caused no further significant change. Measured 30 min after those stretches, which was more than 30 min after the contractions, passive moment and tendon stiffness were still significantly reduced.
why_it_motivates: X01: Passive moment depends on contraction history. Passive trials recorded before the active block, before any strong contractions, may overestimate the passive torque present once the subject has done MVCs (our inference). The reduction was still there more than 30 min later, so it could last through much of a recording session. This supports either re-measuring passive torque after the warm-up and MVC contractions or taking it from rest periods between contractions. It also explains why a table recorded first could be biased in one direction.
comparable_problem: Related technique: how passive ankle moment changes after contractions on a dynamometer. It is not an EMG-to-torque regression study.
does_not_establish: The 4.9% is an average change after maximal contractions. The abstract does not say at which angle passive moment was measured, but it was probably in the stretched, dorsiflexed range. The paper does not give the change in Nm at strongly plantarflexed angles, where passive torque is small. It does not test submaximal tracking contractions, and Duong et al. 2001 found that isometric contractions during a release did not clearly change passive-torque recovery. The 30-min result comes after contractions followed by stretching, so it is not a clean time course of the contraction effect alone. It does not say whether this bias is big enough to explain the R2 drop in our model.
verification_note: Title, authors, journal, volume, issue, pages, DOI and PMID 19644033 confirmed from the PubMed record. All numbers checked against the full PubMed abstract. Full text not read: the publisher page sits behind a Cloudflare challenge, and the ECU and Northampton repository records have no full-text file. So the angle and velocity of the passive-moment measurement are not confirmed. Corrections to the original: (1) the 30-min persistence is measured from the end of the later stretching protocol, not from the contractions; (2) the 21.0% drop is in peak triceps surae EMG amplitude; (3) the earlier claim that the effect lasts 'longer than a session' was an unsupported assumption about our protocol and has been softened.

title: A new method for gravity correction of dynamometer data and determining passive elastic moments at the joint
authors: Anderson DE, Nussbaum MA, Madigan ML
venue: Journal of Biomechanics 43(6):1220-1223
relevant_finding: Dynamometer torque contains muscle torque plus a gravity moment and a passive elastic moment, and both must be estimated and subtracted to isolate the muscle torque. The authors modelled passive torque as a general sinusoid for gravity (A1 sin θ + A2 cos θ) plus two exponential terms for passive tissue, one for each end of the range. They fitted it in steps to slow (5 deg/s) passive sweeps through the full range, two cycles per joint, from 20 healthy older adults aged 55-73 on a Biodex System 3. The gravity term was fitted only within a middle 'gravity-only region' (40% of the range, where passive elastic torque was assumed negligible). The exponentials were then fitted to what was left at each end. Mean concordance with measured passive torque was 0.981 at the ankle. Within the gravity-only region, the ankle RMS error was 0.641 Nm with the new method versus 0.972 Nm with the usual single-point sine method (p<0.001).
why_it_motivates: X01: Rather than a lookup table with one passive value per angle, where a single bad entry corrupts that angle, fit a smooth gravity-plus-exponential curve across the angles for each subject and session. A bad entry then shows up as a clear outlier from the curve and can be replaced by the fitted value. The ankle residuals here (about 0.6-1.0 Nm) are of similar size to the 0.4-0.8 Nm spread of voluntary torque at our plantarflexed angles (our inference). So small passive or gravity errors could swamp the signal at those angles, but not at strong angles where the spread is about 15 Nm.
comparable_problem: Related technique: separating gravity and passive torque from dynamometer data. It is not an EMG-to-torque regression study.
does_not_establish: The subjects were older adults, and the data were dense, continuous slow sweeps rather than static holds at a few fixed angles. Fitting this 6-parameter model to only 8 static points per subject and session is untested and may overfit. Hysteresis was reduced by fitting both sweep directions together, so stress relaxation during a hold is not modelled. The RMS errors are fit residuals in the middle 'gravity-only' region, the same region used for fitting. They are not checked against an independent ground truth and say nothing about the end ranges where the passive exponentials dominate. The gravity-only-region assumption was challenged in a published letter (Clarke, Martin, Herbert 2010, J Biomech 43(13):2653-2655, with an author reply). The paper does not test effects on active torque estimates or on any EMG model.
verification_note: Full text read from the PMC author manuscript (PMC2849864) through NCBI E-utilities. Confirmed: title, authors, J Biomech 43(6):1220-1223, DOI, PMID 20047749, model equations, stepwise fitting (40% gravity-only region, then end exponentials), n=20 older adults aged 55-73, Biodex System 3, 5 deg/s sweeps, mean concordance (0.996 hip, 0.987 knee, 0.981 ankle) and RMS errors within the gravity-only region (ankle 0.641 vs 0.972 Nm, p<0.001). Corrections: the original described 'one smooth model' fitted at once and 'averaging the two sweep directions'. The fit was actually stepwise and used a full cycle, and the averaging of directions applied to the single-point comparison method. The RMS errors are now described as in-sample residuals. PubMed lists two comment letters on this paper: Clarke EC, Martin JH, Herbert R (PMID 20627306), titled 'Assumption of a gravity only region ... may be problematic', and Baltzopoulos V (PMID 20869719). Their text was not read.

title: Mechanomyogram amplitude vs. isometric ankle plantarflexion torque of human medial gastrocnemius muscle at different ankle joint angles
authors: Shi F, Rymer WZ, Son J
venue: Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology 61:102609
relevant_finding: 10 healthy adults did isometric plantarflexion at three ankle angles: 26 deg plantarflexion, 10 deg plantarflexion and 3 deg dorsiflexion. At each angle they did one passive trial, three MVCs and three holds at each of 10, 20, 30, 50 and 70% MVC, with 30-s breaks. Each hold started from rest and was then held at the target for at least 6 s. EMG (MG, LG, SOL, TA), MMG and torque were recorded. Passive torque was estimated as the mean of the first 1 s of filtered torque, averaged over all trials at an angle, so one value per angle per subject rather than one per trial. It was then expressed relative to the 26-deg plantarflexed angle. Passive torque increased significantly as the ankle was dorsiflexed (F(2,27)=25.85, p<0.0001), as did maximum torque (F(2,27)=17.98, p<0.0001). The contraction torque was the mean of a 4-s steady segment. The paper does not describe subtracting passive torque from it.
why_it_motivates: X01: A recent example of taking the passive estimate from the resting start of the contraction trials themselves, at the same angle, rather than relying only on a separate passive trial. That estimate is closer in time and in contraction history to the active data, which addresses the stress-relaxation and recording-order concerns. In X01 the cleaned table could be checked against, or replaced by, pre-contraction rest baselines from our own active trials. Note that Shi et al. averaged these baselines across trials and used them only to describe passive torque, not to correct the voluntary torque.
comparable_problem: Related technique: muscle-signal amplitude (MMG) versus isometric plantarflexion torque at several ankle angles, including a strongly plantarflexed one, in healthy adults. EMG was recorded but used only for a load-sharing ratio. There is no EMG-to-torque model.
does_not_establish: It does not compare passive-torque estimation methods, and it does not show that a rest-baseline estimate is more accurate than a separate passive table. It does not use the passive estimate to correct the voluntary torque. Because the most plantarflexed angle was the zero reference, there is no absolute passive torque at the angle where our model fails. A rest baseline can also include small residual muscle activity before the contraction. It does not address EMG-to-torque model accuracy or session-to-session transfer.
verification_note: Full text read from the PMC author manuscript (PMC8629954) through NCBI E-utilities, and bibliographic data confirmed from PubMed (PMID 34689116). Confirmed: authors, JEK 61:102609, DOI, n=10, the three angles, EMG on MG/LG/SOL/TA, the protocol (one passive trial, 3 MVCs, 5 submaximal levels x 3, 30-s breaks), passive torque as 'an average value of the first 1-s ... in all trials' referenced to P1, and both F statistics. Corrections to the original: (1) passive torque was not estimated per trial; the first-1-s values were averaged across all trials at each angle; (2) the earlier verification note called this an example of 'measuring and subtracting passive torque'. Only P1's passive value was subtracted, to reference passive torque across angles. The text does not describe subtracting passive torque from the contraction torque. (3) The comparable_problem label is changed from 'comparable' to 'related technique', because the main outcome is MMG, not EMG-to-torque. The paper's relevance to X01 is weaker than first stated, but the corrected statements are supported.
